stories.title: PCA 40-40 Chase — Two HRs Away, 25 Games Left (Tier 1 — FOLLOW UP)

x_posts.label: Post 1-1
x_posts.text:
Pete Crow-Armstrong is two home runs away from joining a club with only 5 members.

40 HR + 40 SB in a season: Canseco. Bonds. A-Rod. Soriano. Acuña.

PCA has 25 games to make history. .283/38 HR/32 SB. Cubs at 82-57. This is happening. #Cubs

x_posts.label: Post 1-2
x_posts.text:
PCA needs 8 stolen bases in 25 games for 40-40.

He's averaged a steal every 3-4 games this season. The math works.

The question is whether he gets the green light enough with the Cubs protecting a Wild Card lead. #Cubs #MLB

facebook.long_form:
Window: 9:00 AM ET

Pete Crow-Armstrong is two home runs and eight stolen bases away from one of the rarest achievements in baseball history.

The 40-40 club has exactly five members. Jose Canseco did it first in 1988. Barry Bonds in 1996. Alex Rodriguez in 1998. Alfonso Soriano in 2006. Ronald Acuña Jr. in 2023. That's it. Nineteen years passed between Soriano and Acuña. Three years later, we might be watching it happen again.

PCA enters September at .283 with 38 home runs and 32 stolen bases. He has 25 games left. The math is almost done — but the Cubs (82-57) are fighting for a Wild Card position, and every lineup decision, every green light, every at-bat in a close game carries playoff weight.

That's what makes this different from chasing a milestone on a losing team. PCA isn't just playing for history. He's playing for October. And the Cubs need him for both.

Two home runs. Eight stolen bases. Twenty-five games. This is the most interesting chase in baseball right now.

article.headline: Pete Crow-Armstrong Is Two Home Runs From History — and the Cubs Need Him to Get There

facebook.long_form:
Window: 11:00 AM ET

The morning after a dominant performance is when the baseball world catches up.

Jakub Misiorowski went to Wrigley Field on September 2 and did what he's been doing all season — only louder. Scoreless innings. Eight strikeouts. A peak velocity of 101.5 miles per hour. The velocity concern that had followed him through August? Answered. Definitively.

His season numbers: 14-5, 1.73 ERA, 222 strikeouts, 0.75 WHIP. The Brewers are 87-53 and lead the NL Central. His Cy Young odds sit at -1400. That's not a race. That's a formality waiting to be announced.

The question people keep asking is whether anyone can close the gap. The honest answer is that there isn't a gap — there's a canyon. Misiorowski's ERA is nearly a full run lower than the next closest competitor. His WHIP is historically elite. He's pitching for a team in first place.

His next start projects for September 7 or 8. After what happened at Wrigley, the entire baseball world will be watching.

stories.title: Cardinals 70-70 — After Stunning the Dodgers, What's Next? (Tier 1 — FOLLOW UP)

x_posts.label: Post 3-1
x_posts.text:
Thomas Saggese broke up Yamamoto's no-hitter AND hit the walk-off single in extras.

Cardinals 8, Dodgers 6. St. Louis moves to 70-70.

22 games left. 3.5 out of the Wild Card. They're still alive. #Cardinals #MLB

x_posts.label: Post 3-2
x_posts.text:
70-70 with 22 games left.

Cardinals need to go roughly 14-8 the rest of the way and get help to make October.

Narrow? Yes. Impossible? Not with Saggese playing like this. #Cardinals

facebook.long_form:
Window: 8:30 AM ET

The Cardinals shouldn't still be alive. But Thomas Saggese made sure they are.

On September 3, St. Louis went to Los Angeles and handed the Dodgers their latest loss in a rough stretch. The final: Cardinals 8, Dodgers 6, in 10 innings. The hero: a 23-year-old third baseman who doesn't seem to know what a pressure situation looks like.

Saggese broke up Yoshinobu Yamamoto's no-hit bid in the sixth inning with a two-run home run. Then, in the 10th, he came up with the go-ahead single to give the Cardinals the lead for good. Leo Bernal added his first career MLB home run. Báez contributed a pinch-hit double. It was a full team effort against one of the best arms in the NL.

Now St. Louis sits at 70-70 with 22 games left. They're 3.5 games out of a Wild Card spot. The math requires about a 14-8 finish and help from other teams. That's a narrow road.

But narrow isn't closed. Not with Saggese playing like this.

stories.title: Alvarez Triple Crown — The Math Gets Tighter With 25 Games Left (Tier 2 — FOLLOW UP)

x_posts.label: Post 4
x_posts.text:
Yordan Alvarez leads the AL in batting average, home runs, AND RBIs.

BA: .322 (Simpson .308, 14 back)
HR: 36 (Caminero & Rice at 35, 1 back)
RBI: 91 (tied with Alonso)

25 games. Last AL Triple Crown: Cabrera, 2012. #Astros #MLB

facebook.long_form:
Window: 1:00 PM ET

Yordan Alvarez is leading the American League in batting average, home runs, and RBIs. All three. Simultaneously. With 25 games left.

The Triple Crown is one of baseball's rarest achievements. The last American League player to win it was Miguel Cabrera in 2012. Before that, you have to go back to Carl Yastrzemski in 1967. It happens once in a generation, if that.

Alvarez's current lines: .322 batting average, 36 home runs, 91 RBIs. Every category has a challenger. Simpson sits 14 points back in average at .308. Misael Caminero and Ben Rice are each at 35 home runs, one behind. Pete Alonso has matched the 91 RBI total exactly.

Three leads. Three active threats. Twenty-five games to hold them all.

The pressure here is different from chasing a milestone. Alvarez has to protect three leads at once while opponents go all-out to chase him down. Every game matters in every column. That's the Triple Crown in September.

article.headline: Yordan Alvarez and the Triple Crown That Nobody Seems to Want to Talk About

stories.title: Ohtani's October Cloud — Will the Dodgers Rest Their Star? (Tier 2 — FOLLOW UP)

x_posts.label: Post 5
x_posts.text:
"Not close to optimal."

That's Dave Roberts on Shohei Ohtani — who is 7-for-51 (.137) with 20 strikeouts since Aug. 18.

Left knee. Rest discussions ongoing. Dodgers are 82-57 and safe.

Do they shut him down to get right for October? #Dodgers #MLB

facebook.long_form:
Window: 10:30 PM ET

Dave Roberts said it plainly: Shohei Ohtani is "not close to optimal."

For 17 days, Ohtani has been one of baseball's biggest stories for all the wrong reasons. Since August 18, he's gone 7-for-51 (.137) with 20 strikeouts. On September 3 against the Cardinals — in a game the Dodgers lost 8-6 — he went 0-for-4 with four more strikeouts.

The left knee is the issue. Rest discussions are happening. And the Dodgers, at 82-57 with a playoff spot locked up, now face the central question of their October preparation: do you keep running Ohtani out there through September, or do you sit him down and let him get right?

The argument for resting him is obvious. A healthy Ohtani in October is worth far more than a compromised Ohtani in late September regular season games that don't affect the standings. The argument against is harder to quantify — rust, rhythm, the difficulty of just switching a player of his caliber back on after extended rest.

Roberts hasn't announced a decision. But "not close to optimal" isn't nothing. It's a signal that the Dodgers are thinking seriously about what October needs from their franchise player.

Whatever they decide, Ohtani's health is now the biggest storyline in Los Angeles baseball.
